anchor.after: A couple always consists of two forces acting on the same single rigid body.

visuals.purpose: Establish the four definitive criteria of a couple by contrasting a valid couple on a body with three counterexamples: unequal forces, forces in the same direction, and collinear forces on the same line of action.
visuals.what_to_show: Four comparative horizontal rectangular panels displayed side by side or in a two-by-two grid. Panel 1 shows a valid couple: two parallel forces of equal magnitude F pointing in opposite directions along separate lines with perpendicular separation d. Panel 2 shows unequal forces: one upward force of magnitude F and one downward force of magnitude 2F. Panel 3 shows parallel forces pointing in the same direction: two upward forces of magnitude F. Panel 4 shows collinear forces: two equal and opposite forces of magnitude F pointing directly along the same line of action with zero perpendicular separation. Each panel has clear force arrows, dashed lines of action, and a concise status label.
visuals.what_to_notice: Only Panel 1 meets all four necessary criteria: equal magnitude, opposite direction, parallel lines of action, and separate lines of action. Panel 2 fails equal magnitude; Panel 3 fails opposite direction; Panel 4 fails separate lines of action.

anchor.after: By using the full separation $d$ rather than the distance to the centre, the formula combines both turning effects into one step.

visuals.purpose: Demonstrate the calculation of torque (torque = F * d) on a rotating steering wheel and a straight bar, highlighting the perpendicular separation d between lines of action and showing why the formula uses one force F rather than 2F.
visuals.what_to_show: Two paired diagrams. Left panel shows a circular steering wheel with centre dot O and radius r. Two equal opposite tangential forces of magnitude F act at opposite ends of a vertical diameter, one pointing upward on the left and one downward on the right. Dimension arrows mark the full perpendicular separation d equal to 2r across the diameter, as well as radius r from centre O to each force. A curved arrow shows clockwise rotation. Right panel shows a straight bar of length d with central pivot O. Opposite forces of magnitude F act at the ends with perpendicular separation d. Annotations show that summing moments about the centre (F * d/2 + F * d/2) produces the identical result F * d.
visuals.what_to_notice: The perpendicular separation d spans the full distance between the two lines of action. Using one force F with the full separation d accounts completely for the total turning effect of both forces without doubling.

heading_path: Finding the perpendicular separation across different geometries
anchor.after: Measure only the distance between the two points where the parallel force lines cross the beam.

visuals.purpose: Deconstruct perpendicular distance determination across three key examination contexts: (1) tangential forces on a disc of radius r giving separation 2r; (2) inclined forces on a right-angled plate showing perpendicular side y versus hypotenuse x; and (3) forces acting at points along an offset rod.
visuals.what_to_show: Three distinct panels. Panel 1 depicts a circular disc with two parallel vertical tangential forces of magnitude F at opposite edges, showing diameter 2r as the perpendicular separation between lines of action with a right-angle marker. Panel 2 depicts a right-angled triangular plate with parallel opposite forces F acting at vertices V and W; dashed lines extend the lines of action, highlighting the perpendicular side length y with a right-angle marker and crossing out the hypotenuse length x. Panel 3 depicts a horizontal rod of total length L with forces F applied at interior points separated by distance d, explicitly marking d as the relevant separation and dimming the unused end segments.
visuals.what_to_notice: In every geometry, torque calculation requires the shortest 90-degree distance between the parallel lines of action. For a disc, this is the diameter 2r, not the radius r. For an angled plate, it is the perpendicular side y, not the diagonal hypotenuse x. For an offset rod, it is the force separation d, not the total rod length L.

anchor.after: The body experiences the exact same angular acceleration regardless of where the couple is mounted.

visuals.purpose: Illustrate the translational invariance of a couple: display a rigid bar with a couple in Position 1 and translated to Position 2, demonstrating that the torque about any reference point remains identical because force magnitude and separation are unchanged.
visuals.what_to_show: A comparative diagram showing a rigid horizontal bar in two configurations: Position 1 and Position 2. In Position 1, a couple with forces F separated by distance d acts near the left end of the bar. In Position 2, the exact same couple (identical force magnitudes F and identical separation d) has been translated to the right end of the bar. An arrow labelled 'translated along rigid bar' connects the two. Below both configurations, an arbitrary external reference point P is marked, with dashed lines and calculated moment equations confirming that the net torque about P equals F * d in both positions.
visuals.what_to_notice: The torque produced by a couple does not depend on where the couple is located on a rigid body. Because the force magnitudes F and perpendicular separation d are unchanged, translating the couple produces the exact same rotational effect.
